supplement.where: Appendices A to F, pp. 13-31 of this PDF; code at https://github.com/GeMoLLM/GeMO (p. 5, p. 13)
supplement.holds: Sampling parameters and generation length (A, p. 13); source-data construction, persona list, and word-processing steps (B, p. 14); perplexity filter, high-temperature results (Fig. 6), topic shifts (Fig. 7), pre-trained Llama-2 (Fig. 8), OpenAI models (Fig. 9), temperature decay (Fig. 10), the word-choice entropy heatmap (Fig. 11), unique-word counts (Table 2), and Figs. 12-13 (C, pp. 14-21); coding details (D, pp. 20-22); plagiarism examples, prompt trials, the authors' check of GPT-3.5 code summaries (Table 3, p. 24), and the full GPT-4 and Claude-3-Sonnet coding results, Figs. 20-29 (E, pp. 22-31); compute and licenses (F, pp. 26 and 31). No standard errors, confidence intervals, or inferential tests are reported in the main text or appendices.

paper_design_summary: The authors compare LLM-generated book reviews and Python solutions with existing human-written Goodreads reviews and CodeContests solutions; no people are assigned to AI assistance. After corpus filtering, the review study analyzed 742 books with 10 human reviews per book and up to 10 generated reviews per book and setting; the coding study analyzed 100 Codeforces level-A problems with 20 sampled correct human solutions per problem (pp. 6-7; App. B.1, p. 14). Scored attributes include review sentiment, topic and word choice, plus code similarity, complexity, runtime dispersion and correctness.

studies.label: Book reviews: LLM-generated vs Goodreads human reviews

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. LLM-generated reviews (gen) are compared with existing human-written Goodreads reviews (src) of the same books; model, sampling parameters, and prompt vary by design.
assignment.quote: we compare the diversity in sentiment of Goodreads reviews [12] (i.e., src)—very likely a portion of LLM training data [13]—with LLM-generated reviews (i.e., gen).
assignment.locator: p. 1, Section 1; p. 4, Section 4.1; pp. 5-6, Section 6.1

arms.name: gen (LLM-generated reviews)
arms.description: Llama-2-13b, Llama-2-13b-chat, Vicuna-13b-v1.5, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (0914), GPT-4-turbo (0125). For each combination of model, sampling setting (T in {0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5}, top-p in {0.90, 0.95, 0.98, 1.00}) and prompt ((1) plain or (2) celebrity persona), 10 samples were generated per book. After excluding reviews with perplexity above 20, up to 10 reviews per book and setting were analyzed (m_i <= 10; p. 6; App. C.1, p. 14).

arms.name: src (Goodreads human reviews)
arms.description: Analyzed corpus after filtering: 742 books with English titles, with 10 existing Goodreads reviews per book of 300 to 700 words (p. 6; App. B.1, p. 14).

participants.exclusions: No human study participants. Corpus filtering: books with 1,000 to 2,500 reviews (750 books), non-English titles dropped, reviews limited to 300-700 words, and 10 reviews sampled per book; 742 books were analyzed after filtering (App. B.1, p. 14). Generated reviews with perplexity above 20 were excluded (p. 6; App. C.1, p. 14).
participants.who: No human study participants. The analyzed human-review corpus covers 742 books with 10 existing Goodreads reviews each; the paper does not count or describe the reviewers (p. 6; App. B.1, p. 14).
participants.quote: craft a final dataset of N = 742 books with English titles, and ∀i, ni = 10 reviews per book such that the review length is between 300 and 700 words.

ai_tool.how_used: The models write the reviews themselves; no person uses AI. Prompt (1): 'Write a personalized review of the book titled {title}:'; prompt (2): 'Write a book review for the book titled {title} as if you are {person}:', with 10 celebrity personas (App. B.2, p. 14). Nucleus sampling with T in {0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5} and top-p in {0.90, 0.95, 0.98, 1.00} (p. 6); at most 500 new tokens (App. A, p. 13); a temperature-decay variant runs T from 10.0 to 1.2 over the first 50 tokens (p. 5).

task.description: Write a review of a named popular book (Goodreads books with 1,000 to 2,500 reviews). Reviews are compared on the dispersion of sentiment, topic, and word choice, not judged for creativity.

outcomes.name: Sentiment: distribution across books of the per-book mean sentiment, and per-book sentiment entropy
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: A fine-tuned DistilBERT SST-2 classifier labels each review 0 or 1 (p. 6; 91.3% accuracy on the SST-2 dev set). Mean and entropy are computed over each book's reviews (conditional distribution) and shown across books as stacked bars of mean-sentiment ranges and entropy histograms. Variants by sampling parameters, prompt, model, and temperature decay: Fig. 4(a)-(c) (p. 8), Fig. 6 (p. 16), Fig. 8 (p. 17), Fig. 9 (p. 18), Fig. 10 (p. 19), Figs. 12-13 (pp. 20-21). The classifier is a sentiment model, not a creativity scorer.

contrasts.reported: Share of books with mean sentiment in (0.95,1.00], prompt (1), T = 1.2, p = 1.0: source 2.8%, Llama-2 (pre-trained) 5.9%, Vicuna-13b 44.7%, Llama-2-chat 82.1% (p. 9; Fig. 4(c), p. 8). 'for both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, 100% of the samples have average positivity falling in (0.95,1.00] under prompt (1), and 98.9% and 97.6% under prompt (2)' (pp. 7-8; Fig. 9, p. 18, at T = 1.2, p = 1.0). The text prints these shares; everything else is in figures. No SDs or tests.
contrasts.locator: pp. 7-9, Section 7, Takeaways 1 and 3; p. 8, Fig. 4(a)-(c); p. 18, Fig. 9

contrasts.treatment_arm: Llama-2-chat, prompt (2) celebrity persona, T = 1.2, p = 1.0
contrasts.reported: Model-only contrast with no people. Prompt (2) 'reduces the percentage of the most positive range from 82.1% to 58.1% in Fig. 4(b) for T = 1.2, p = 1.0. However, the gap is still large.' Source share 2.8% (p. 9).

diversity_detail.metric: Distribution over books of the per-book mean sentiment (share of books in each range); per-book entropy of the 0/1 sentiment labels
diversity_detail.computed_over: Within each book: the 10 source reviews vs up to 10 generated reviews per setting (conditional distribution); distribution shown over the 742 books
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; descriptive figures and shares only
diversity_detail.notes: Lower dispersion in gen means less diverse. The comparison sets one model's samples against reviews by many human reviewers, not people working with and without AI.

outcomes.name: Topic: per-book topic entropy and unconditional top-10 topic distribution
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: BERTopic pre-trained on Wikipedia (MaartenGr/BERTopic_Wikipedia) assigns each review one of about 2,000 topics (p. 6). Entropy of the topics within each book (conditional), shown as KDE across books; shares of the top 10 topics over all reviews (unconditional). Fig. 4(d)-(e) (p. 8), Fig. 7 (p. 17), Figs. 8-10 (pp. 17-19), Figs. 12-13 (pp. 20-21).

contrasts.reported: Figure only; no values printed. Fig. 4 caption: 'the model-generated reviews are overwhelmingly positive and cover a narrower range of the topics per book; moreover, there is distinctive under- and over-representation of the topics covered overall.' App. C.3: topic group 15 ('rob', 'kill') is under-represented; groups 333 and 666 are over-represented.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Fig. 4(d)-(e) and caption; p. 15, App. C.3; p. 17, Fig. 7

diversity_detail.metric: Entropy of topic labels within each book; top-10 topic shares over all reviews
diversity_detail.embedding_model: BERTopic (MaartenGr/BERTopic_Wikipedia), used as a topic classifier
diversity_detail.computed_over: Reviews of each book within a condition (conditional); all reviews in a condition pooled (unconditional)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; KDE plots and bar charts only
diversity_detail.notes: Lower entropy in gen means less diverse.

outcomes.name: Word choice: count of unique words and entropy of the word distribution (unconditional)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: All reviews in a condition are concatenated, lowercased, contraction-expanded, tokenized with NLTK word_tokenize, stripped of punctuation and non-alphabetic tokens, and lemmatized with WordNetLemmatizer (App. B.3, p. 14). Count of unique words: Table 2 (p. 19), Llama-2-chat and GPT-3.5, prompt (1), T in {0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2} by top-p in {0.90, 0.95, 0.98, 1.00}. Entropy of the word distribution: Fig. 11 heatmap (p. 19), Llama-2-chat and Vicuna-13b, prompts (1) and (2), same grid.

contrasts.reported: Unique words (Table 2, prompt (1)): source 85,334; Llama-2-chat 18,900 (T = 0.5, p = 0.90) to 33,908 (T = 1.2, p = 1.00); GPT-3.5 15,778 (T = 0.5, p = 0.98) to 21,059 (T = 1.2, p = 1.00). Word-choice entropy (Fig. 11 cell values): source 9.99; Llama-2-chat and Vicuna-13b generations 8.90 to 9.75 across the grid. One value per configuration; no SDs or tests.

diversity_detail.metric: Number of unique lemmatized words; entropy of the word-frequency distribution
diversity_detail.computed_over: All reviews in a condition pooled (unconditional distribution)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; one value per configuration
diversity_detail.notes: Generated sets can hold fewer than 10 reviews per book after the perplexity filter (m_i <= 10, p. 6); the paper states no adjustment of the counts for corpus size.

studies.label: Code solutions: LLM-generated vs CodeContests human solutions

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. LLM-generated Python solutions (gen) are compared with existing human-written solutions from CodeContests (src) for the same Codeforces problems.
assignment.quote: the range of algorithms employed in (correct) solutions to a given coding problem (i.e., gen) was much less varied than a sample of human answers (src) available on the web [14]
assignment.locator: p. 2, Section 1; p. 4, Section 4.1; pp. 6-7, Section 6.2

arms.name: gen (LLM-generated solutions)
arms.description: GPT-4 (k = 100 samples per problem) and Claude-3-Sonnet (k = 200), T in {0.5, 1.0}, top-p in {0.9, 1.0}; at least 20 correct solutions per problem (p. 7). All outcomes except accuracy use correct solutions only (p. 7).

arms.name: src (CodeContests human solutions)
arms.description: 100 level-A Codeforces problems, 20 randomly sampled correct python3 solutions per problem (p. 6). Source accuracy uses the CodeContests counts of correct and all solutions (App. D.3, pp. 21-22).

participants.exclusions: No participants. Restricted to 100 level-A (easiest) Codeforces problems and python3 solutions (p. 6; App. D.1, pp. 20-21). All code outcomes except accuracy use correct solutions only (p. 7).
participants.who: No human participants. The human outputs are existing CodeContests solutions (100 problems, 20 randomly sampled correct python3 solutions each); the paper does not count or describe the programmers.
participants.quote: We limited the scope to a subset (N = 100) of level-A problems (easy problems) on Codeforces [42], and the language of the solutions to python3.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4-turbo (0125) (called GPT-4) and Claude-3-Sonnet; GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct (0914) extracts code summaries and complexity
ai_tool.how_used: The models write the solutions themselves; no person uses AI. Prompt: 'Please read the below problem description and generate a python code to solve the problem {problem description} Please only generate code and nothing else.' (p. 7). T in {0.5, 1.0}, top-p in {0.9, 1.0}; at most 2048 new tokens (App. A, p. 13).

task.description: Generate Python solutions to Codeforces level-A competitive programming problems. The paper scores correctness, efficiency and diversity of implementations; it does not rate the solutions for creativity (pp. 6-7, Section 6.2).

outcomes.name: Plagiarism score: mean pairwise fingerprint similarity of the solutions to each problem
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: COPYDETECT winnowing fingerprints; mean pairwise similarity over all pairs of correct solutions to a problem (p. 5, Section 4.3; p. 7). Fig. 5(b) (p. 9), Fig. 20 right (GPT-4, p. 28), Fig. 25 right (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 29); example pairs in App. E.1 (pp. 22-24).

contrasts.reported: Figure only (histogram and KDE; no values printed). Text: 'the plagiarism scores of the LLM-generated code are extremely high (Fig. 5(b)), compared to the source solutions which achieve an utterly zero plagiarism score for all the problems.' App. E.6: 'The plagiarism scores achieved by Claude-3 remain high, similarly to that on GPT-4.' Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 7, Takeaway 1; p. 9, Fig. 5(b); p. 26, App. E.6; p. 28, Fig. 20; p. 29, Fig. 25

diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of correct solutions to the same problem within a condition; distribution over the 100 problems
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; histograms and KDE only
diversity_detail.notes: Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.

outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-3.5 writes text summaries of each correct solution (prompt in App. D.5, p. 22), embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2; mean pairwise cosine similarity within each problem (p. 7). Fig. 5(e) shows the description field (p. 9); Figs. 23 (GPT-4, p. 29) and 28 (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 30) show all four fields.

App. E.6 on Claude-3 code summaries: 'Similar to GPT-4, Claude-3 also demonstrate a narrower range of expressed ideas.' Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.

diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of correct solutions to the same problem within a condition; distribution over the 100 problems
diversity_detail.notes: Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.

outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-3.5 assigns tags (from the CodeContests tag list), algorithms, and data structures (from fixed lists) to each correct solution (App. D.5, p. 22); mean pairwise Jaccard index within each problem (p. 7). Fig. 5(f) shows algorithms (p. 9); Figs. 24 (GPT-4, p. 29) and 29 (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 31) show all three; Fig. 1 right previews it for GPT-4 (p. 1).

Text: 'Fig. 5(f) shows the Jaccard similarity of the generated solutions in terms of the inferred algorithms, with the majority of problems displaying high similarity across generated solutions.' Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 7, Takeaway 1; p. 1, Fig. 1 (right); p. 9, Fig. 5(f); p. 29, Fig. 24; p. 31, Fig. 29

diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of correct solutions to the same problem within a condition; distribution over the 100 problems
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; stacked bar charts only
diversity_detail.notes: Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diversity.

outcomes.name: Asymptotic time and space complexity: per-problem entropy and unconditional distribution
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-3.5 infers the big-O time and space complexity of each correct solution (p. 7; prompt in App. D.5, p. 22). Entropy of the complexity classes within each problem (conditional) and histogram over all solutions (unconditional). Fig. 5(c)-(d) (p. 9) shows time complexity; Figs. 21 (GPT-4, p. 28) and 26 (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 30) show time and space.

contrasts.reported: Figure only (histograms; no values printed). Captions of Fig. 21 (GPT-4) and Fig. 26 (Claude-3-Sonnet): 'The figures suggest that the generated code is more efficient than the source code, while showing a decrease in diversity.'

diversity_detail.metric: Entropy of the inferred complexity classes
diversity_detail.computed_over: Correct solutions to the same problem within a condition (conditional); all correct solutions pooled (unconditional)
diversity_detail.notes: Lower entropy in gen means less diverse.

outcomes.name: Runtime and memory dispersion: within-problem standard deviation of runtime and peak memory
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Each correct solution runs on the problem's 10 test cases under /usr/bin/time; the maximum elapsed time (%E) and maximum resident set size (%M) across the 10 cases proxy runtime and memory (App. D.4, p. 22). The SD is taken within each problem's set of correct solutions (conditional distribution, p. 7) and shown as histograms across problems: Fig. 22 (GPT-4, p. 28) and Fig. 27 (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 30). A program-execution measurement, not a creativity scorer.

contrasts.reported: Figure only (histograms; no values printed). The text makes no runtime-specific statement; Takeaway 1 says 'there exists significant narrowing from the source to generation distribution in all attributes considered for both scenarios' (p. 7), and runtime efficiency is one of the listed attributes (Fig. 3, p. 6).
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Fig. 3; p. 7, Section 6.2 (Metric Calculation) and Section 7, Takeaway 1; p. 28, Fig. 22; p. 30, Fig. 27

diversity_detail.metric: Standard deviation of runtime (ms) and of peak memory (KB) within a problem
diversity_detail.computed_over: Correct solutions to the same problem within a condition; histogram over problems
diversity_detail.notes: Lower SD in gen means less diverse. The figures drop runtimes above 200 ms and memory above 30,000 KB for display. The runtime and memory means are efficiency levels and are recorded in notes, not here.

outcomes.name: Correctness: per-problem accuracy (share of solutions passing all 10 test cases)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Simulated autojudge: a solution is correct if it passes all 10 test cases from the dataset (App. D.2, p. 21). Accuracy per problem is n_correct / n_all for the source, from CodeContests counts, and n_correct / k for the generations (App. D.3, pp. 21-22). Uses all solutions, not only correct ones (p. 7). Stacked bars over problems: Fig. 5(a) (p. 9), Fig. 20 left (GPT-4, p. 28), Fig. 25 left (Claude-3-Sonnet, p. 29). A quality measure, not a creativity or diversity score.

contrasts.control_arm: src (CodeContests human solutions, correct and incorrect)
contrasts.reported: 'LLM-generated code segments (a) are over 2× more accurate than the average human solutions' (p. 8). For Claude-3-Sonnet the text compares only with GPT-4: 'the accuracy of Claude-3 is much lower' (p. 26). Stacked bars only; no values printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 7, Takeaway 2; p. 9, Fig. 5(a); p. 26, App. E.6; p. 28, Fig. 20; p. 29, Fig. 25

company_involvement.description: Authors at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Barnard College (p. 1). The PDF has no acknowledgment, funding, or competing-interest statement. The commercial models are objects of study, with no stated company role.

data_and_code.data_url: Goodreads: https://mengtingwan.github.io/data/goodreads.html; CodeContests: https://github.com/google-deepmind/code_contests (p. 31, App. F.2, footnotes 8 and 10)

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: no people are assigned to AI assistance; models generate outputs for comparison with existing human corpora (p. 4, Section 4.1; pp. 5-7, Section 6). Criterion 2 is not met: there is no human participant sample; the reported 742 books and 100 coding problems are corpus units, and unique human authors are not counted (p. 6, Sections 6.1-6.2; p. 14, App. B.1). Criterion 3 is not met under the current codebook's requirement for output that study participants produce: diversity is scored on archival human texts and model generations, so the outcome-level scored_on_output fields remain true without establishing a qualifying participant outcome (p. 4, Sections 4.1-4.3; pp. 6-7, Section 6). Retain ai_vs_human context under codebook Section 3 because the paper directly compares AI-generated and human-generated outputs. No unresolved source question changes any criterion.

one_line_finding: LLM-generated book reviews and code are less diverse than human-written ones: under prompt (1) at T = 1.2 and top-p = 1.0, 82.1 percent of books get Llama-2-chat reviews with mean sentiment in (0.95,1.00] against 2.8 percent for the Goodreads reviews (p. 9; Fig. 4(c), p. 8), and Llama-2-chat reviews use at most 33,908 unique words across the Table 2 settings against 85,334 in the source (p. 19); the paper has no human participants and reports no inferential statistics.
open_questions: The text gives '98.9% and 97.6% under prompt (2)' for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 without 'respectively' (p. 8), and Fig. 9 (p. 18) prints no values, so the form does not assign the two values to models.

For Claude-3-Sonnet, App. E.6 (p. 26) says the solutions 'are less efficient than source solutions', while the Fig. 26 caption (p. 30) repeats the GPT-4 caption that 'the generated code is more efficient than the source code'. Both captions report a decrease in diversity, so the S2-O4 direction does not depend on this conflict.
notes: Locators are PDF pages, which match the printed page numbers. Not listed as outcomes: runtime and memory means, which are efficiency levels (Takeaway 2, p. 8: LLM code uses 'less runtime and memory during execution'; Figs. 22 and 27), and the fraction of valid generations by sampling setting (Table 1, p. 9), a quality filter. Model-only contrasts (temperature, top-p, temperature decay, pre-trained vs aligned Llama-2, Llama-2-chat vs Vicuna-13b) are not separate outcomes; the persona-prompt contrast is kept in S1-O1 because the text prints its numbers, and the per-model shares appear in the S1-O1 gen-vs-source contrast. Table 3 (p. 24) is the authors' 1-to-3 check of GPT-3.5 code summaries on 20 solutions, a validation of attribute extraction, not an outcome. The open-source code models (CodeLlama, StarCoder) produced no solutions and were dropped (App. E.4, p. 26). The paper cites Padmakumar and He on essays written with LLM help (p. 3) but runs no human study. Final review: the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-F, was read; recorded numerical results and eligibility passages were checked against PDF text and printed figure labels. No c025 challenge files were present. Context placement and criterion-3 interpretation were settled using the current codebook; the two remaining reporting ambiguities do not affect eligibility.

differences.resolved: other, as in A. The models write reviews of named books, and the paper scores only the dispersion of sentiment, topic, and word choice, not creativity. The codebook's creative_writing covers stories, poems, essays judged for creativity, slogans, and advertisements; its clause admitting other writing tasks rests on answering across_people, which this design cannot do. The reconciled c011 (peer reviews) and c009 (abstracts) code such writing as other.

differences.resolved: Empty string, as in A. Neither study has participants. The c004 and c019 reconciliations made the same call.

open_items.item: Original context-placement question: settled as ai_vs_human under codebook Section 3. The paper compares existing human-written corpora with model-generated responses (p. 4, Section 4.1; pp. 5-7, Section 6). This context label does not make any core eligibility criterion met; nothing further is needed.

Original criterion-3 interpretation question: settled for c025 as not_met under the current codebook's participant-output requirement. The paper uses archival human corpora and model generations, with no human study participants (p. 4, Section 4.1; pp. 5-7, Section 6). Although this question concerned criterion 3, no uncertainty about that criterion remains; harmonizing other papers is outside this paper's eligibility decision.

Unresolved model-specific assignment of the 98.9% and 97.6% positivity shares under prompt (2): the text lists both percentages without 'respectively' (pp. 7-8, Takeaway 1), and Fig. 9 (p. 18) has no printed bar values. Labeled posted results would settle the mapping; retain the paired statement without assigning individual values to models. No eligibility criterion depends on this mapping.

Unresolved Claude-3-Sonnet efficiency conflict: App. E.6 (p. 26) says its solutions are less efficient than source solutions, but the Fig. 26 caption (p. 30) says more efficient. Author clarification would settle which efficiency statement is intended. This concerns efficiency levels, not the reported diversity direction or any eligibility criterion.
